utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. When we were at the end of the sitting, the issue was discussed about the Chamber's position in respect of witness -- a protected witness, P019, whom the Defence of Mr. Mrksic wishes to give evidence, a witness formerly on the 65 ter list of the Prosecution but who was not called by the Prosecution, and the Defence now of Mr. Mrksic desires to have him. To facilitate the preparation for the Defence, the Chamber was prepared to lend support to efforts to have Witness P019 give evidence by issuing a subpoena. That subpoena is of course, by necessity, then placed in the hands of the government where the witness is living, and it was duly served. Apparently to the Defence the witness indicated that he would not attend. Telephone, informal inquiries, by the witness unit here received a response that he was not prepared to attend under any circumstances. The Chamber has therefore evaluated, at the request of Mr. Vasic, whether in the present circumstances as they are known to the Chamber there is justification for the Chamber to seek to take any further steps in an effort to request the attendance of the witness. Now, present appreciation is that those steps would only be possible if we were prepared to order the commencement of contempt proceedings against the witness for his failure to respond to the subpoena and then proceed to have the government of the country where he lives effect his arrest and transfer. That is a dramatic step in any trial for a witness of a party. It's certainly a dramatic step in an International Tribunal where it is necessary to invoke such powers and compulsive process to ensure the attendance of a witness. So dramatic it is perceived that our research has indicated that no case in the whole history of the Tribunal where that has occurred at the instance of Prosecution or the Defence. This Chamber refused such an application made by the Prosecution in the last trial which we heard. There was a recent case where the Chamber itself in another trial concluded that it was essential in the interests of justice that a small number of witnesses who had not been called by either party should give evidence, and one of those witnesses refused to attend and the Chamber in the end instituted contempt proceedings. They did not proceed because the witness in the circumstances was persuaded to cooperate and did attend. We have looked in particular at what is provided to us as an indication of the evidence which the Defence expects to receive from the witness, and we note that it is based essentially on identification of various positions which the witness is known to have held and to suggest from that that the witness ought to be able to give evidence about various events. We have also noted the summary provided by the Prosecution when that witness was on their list, and we note there that the evidence of that witness focussed primarily on one other of the accused, not on Mr. Mrksic. The nature of the material by way of summary which the Defence of Mr. Mrksic has placed before us does not provide any basis upon which we could conclude on what is presently known to us, that the evidence of this witness is in some way vital to the question of the guilt or innocence of Mr. Mrksic. There's no question that the witness ought to be able to give relevant evidence, but we would perceive that it ought to be a matter of very substantial significance in the trial before we consider there was justification for taking the most unusual step of attempting to achieve the compulsory attendance of the witness. In those circumstances the Chamber has not been persuaded that it should initiate any action at the present time in respect of Witness P019, with a view to ensuring under compulsion the attendance of that witness to give evidence. Now, Mr. Domazet, you -- we advised or arranged for you to be advised verbally yesterday of the decision which we have just given. We understood that you were considering whether some further motion or action might be taken by you, and therefore we would be grateful if you could indicate whether that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Mrksic indeed believes that the testimony of Witness P019 is very important, and as a result of that following my consultations with Mr. Vasic I can convey to you the position of the Defence, namely that we insist that this witness be heard. In the alternative we could accept his testimony to be given via videolink, if it is his travel to The Hague that is the most problematic. However, I would like to say first several things in regard to his readiness or lack thereof to come to The Hague. First of all, I'd like to remind you that he already testified in- the Dokmanovic case, so he was a witness there. When he was placed on the OTP 65 ter list, there must have been some conversation carried with him and he must have given his consent. According to the information we had from that period of time, from the period of time of the Prosecution case - perhaps I'm not right, in which case Mr. Moore can correct me - we had some information that he was actually here in The Hague but ultimately did not testify. Perhaps the Prosecution can confirm this. This might not be the most relevant thing, but nevertheless we believe there are currently no reasons for this witness not to appear here. It is possible that he thought that the medical certificate would be enough to excuse him from coming here. I think that that certificate is not a sufficient excuse. And if he were to be told that that is an insufficient excuse, then I think that would make him think hard about the consequences that might ensue. Perhaps he was under the impression that the medical certificate was sufficient to excuse him from his duty to come here and testify, and if told otherwise perhaps he would be -- that would convince him to come here. Unfortunately, we were unable to get into touch with this witness, first of all because he's a protected witness and he had no particulars about him; and when we sought them, the Prosecution informed us that the witness did not consent to have this information released to Defence. So the first time we received this information was in the subpoena. It was then that we saw where he resides, and prior to that we thought that he resided abroad. However, to this day, we did not establish contact with this witness. It is possible that this witness is hostile to the Defence. But regardless of that, in view of the facts that he can testify about, in view of the documents that we have prepared for his testimony, we believe that it is essential to have this witness testify. By your leave I would give you some details, some further details, but I think that we need to do this in private session in order not to put him at risk -- or rather, his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will go into private session for a little while, Mr. Domazet, to enable you to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, thank you for that. Can you tell us what it is that you now propose. Are you moving a specific motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have already issued a subpoena for this witness. I'm not sure that the witness is aware of the fact that his excuse for not coming to testify here is not justified; therefore, perhaps we should make another attempt. We as the Defence are not in the position to do that. We are banned from contacting him, but perhaps another service could get in touch with him and explain to him that the medical reasons put forward by him are not sufficient to relieve him of his duty to come here and testify. As I have said to you, if it is problematic for him to travel to The Hague, we agree to have him testify via videolink, but it means that we would have to reschedule his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, why do you say that you are banned from contacting the witness you propose to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, we, the Defence, in the past asked for contact information of this witness, and the Prosecution in an e-mail told us that the witness did not consent to have his information released to us so that we could contact him. Perhaps the registry could do that, could provide his information to us, perhaps you can give us an approval to contact him, and if that is the case we will contact him. And if necessary, one of us can travel to Zagreb and try to talk to him, because we truly believe that it is very important. And perhaps he could consent in that case in order to avoid all the unpleasant consequences that might ensue, the ones that you described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, one issue that arose was whether you should be provided by order with what was confidential information. You now have the contact details; what is to stop you speaking to the witness you intend to call? There is nothing I think you'll find, Mr. Domazet. You are not subject to any order precluding you contacting potential witnesses. There was a different issue perhaps when this was a witness about to be called by the Prosecution and subject to protection orders, but that time has passed. He's now a witness you wish to call. But let me tell you something more. The witness has been formally advised of the consequences of noncompliance with the subpoena. He has indicated by telephone that he has no intention of attending. He places no basis in his medical certificate for that position. He is clearly not prepared to give evidence, at least at your instigation. Now, the Chamber is faced with the position, which we discussed in the reasons we delivered a few moments ago, whether we should see that his attendance was so important as to justify the Chamber taking further compulsory -- well, attempting further compulsory action. And we can only, we think, do so by taking the further step of charging him with contempt. And as I've indicated, what is before us at the moment does not persuade us to that effect. You have put some further matters now in your submissions, but we are of the view that they are matters which we have considered. We have no doubt that he could give relevant evidence, but what we were looking for was some aspect of his evidence which is of great significance to the question of guilt or innocence of your client and which is not able to be the subject of other evidence. Many of the matters have already been the subject of evidence in the course of the evidence we've received. The thought that he might give a different version doesn't mean that his different evidence is in some way vital, because the subject matters that you've been talking about in most cases are dealing with the general background circumstances. They are relevant, but they are not going to the vital issues of guilt or innocence of your client. You spoke that this witness has indicated that he had negotiations with Colonel Mrksic. We don't know anything of those negotiations so far, we've not heard of them from other witnesses, but there are clearly likely to be many other witnesses who are aware of those negotiations and present at them, including your client. But we have no evidence of them. You have not even suggested that this witness was in Vukovar at the time of the offences which are the subject of the charges. And as you may know, his evidence in Dokmanovic was to the contrary. Therefore, we do not see at the moment that there is that degree of great significance which would require this Tribunal to take whatever steps it could to try and get the witness to give evidence. You mentioned he could evidence by videolink; of course he could, but only if he is prepared to attend to give that evidence. And his position, as far as we are aware of it is that he is simply not prepared to give evidence. We have no means of compelling his attendance in another country before a videolink position so that we can hear him by videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it, Mr. Domazet, that you are moving that we should take some formal action? And if so, is it that we should institute proceedings for contempt? Or what is it that you wish? Do we misunderstand our legal powers? I know these are hard questions and I'm sorry to put them to you, but this is a matter where we need to have a very clear indication of positions for very clearly articulated reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have heard your explanation and I have heard things that I wasn't aware of. If the only justification that this witness has for not appearing is the medical certificate, that's one thing; but now you have just informed me that this witness has refused to testify altogether. These circumstances are new to us and the Defence expects the Chamber to take all other measures still remaining, not only for the sake of this witness's testimony but also for the sake of future witnesses' credibility, the witnesses appearing at this Tribunal. We believe it is of great importance to put the point across that all those summoned by the court must appear. As for the conversations with Colonel Mrksic, maybe I could add a word or two about that since there are no other witnesses to those conversations. This testimony was obtained by a phone line through three different countries and this is something that the witness should tell us about. And only he can explain what and how was agreed. Therefore, to sum it up, the Defence stands by its request to have this witness brought here to testify. It is down to the Chamber eventually to decide whether contempt proceedings should be set in motion. We as the Defence do believe that this witness has submitted a violation and that he has no sufficient justification for refusing to appear before this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. Is there anything that any other Defence counsel would wish to put? Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. Witness P019 was of interest to the other Defence teams, especially when he was still on the 65 ter list of the OTP. Let us not forget the fact that it was I of all people on behalf of Miroslav Radic's Defence TO who moved to tender into evidence the document produced by the Croatian secret services about an incursion into OTP documents when this witness was about to appear, and it was only after that that the indictments were confirmed in relation to all three of the accused. So he was a relevant witness. But the Radic Defence believes that pressure exerted on any witness by whoever - pressure exerted for a witness to appear and testify - is in principle harmful and counter-productive. As a matter of principle, I would oppose any motion to all practical intents for -- to compel any witness to appear and give evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my understanding if you were paying close attention when looking at the 65 ter summaries of the OTP, and I understand exactly what you are focussing on in your statement. As for the witness, I can only say the same thing as Mr. Borovic. I would have been greatly interested in cross-examining this witness had he appeared as a witness. All I can say now is what the position of my client is. I was going to say this later, but it's relevant at this point. The position of Mr. Sljivancanin about witnesses, when we were making our decisions as to who we would be calling was that we would only be calling witnesses who agree to appear of their own free will; that was a guiding principle for us. As for this particular case, I believe the matter should be resolved between the party calling the witness, intending to call the witness, and the Chamber. As a result, we do not have any specific position on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Moore, is there any submission for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If the Court is not minded to grant the application of my learned friend, we would have no submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If we were minded or were considering it, what would be your submission, Mr. Moore? We look for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I will endeavour to assist the Court. Even though a witness may indicate that his reason for not giving evidence is his own personal view, in my submission a Court cannot move away from a medical certificate which is clearly legitimate and valid which of itself tends to suggest that there may be a renewed deterioration of his mental state and the consequence of the traumatic effects, because that clearly may go to the application of his own judgement whether he gives evidence or does not. That is point one. The second is this: This witness clearly was on the Prosecution list, and it was the Prosecution intention to call this witness. My learned friends are aware that he did attend. The Prosecution then decided not to call him, and it may well be that the Court might take the view that those who saw him perhaps took the view which would be comparable to the medical certificate that now appears before the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything further?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Nothing further, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On the question of power?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, in relation to the exercise of the power, the Court should look at the efforts made by the party calling to assess whether there has been good and valid reason for him to be called, whether in actual fact it can be duplicated in other respects, and whether there has been a legitimate and valid attempt by the calling party to call the witness himself. The Prosecution case concluded in June. We did not know if the Defence intended to call that witness or not. It was perfectly open to my learned friends to do that which I did, to check whether in actual fact that person was in the telephone directory at the location where he lives. I was able to do that. I was able to locate that person, being the only person of that name. It was done within five minutes, and my learned friend nevertheless does not seem to accept that it was possible or capable to approach that witness. I'm afraid, I must submit, that my learned friends have not made a vigorous or genuine efforts to call this witness and are using the Court as a means to replace their own rather inadequate attempts. In my submission, the Court does have the power, but it should be exercised very sparingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On what basis does it have the power?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In my submission, the Court would have the power surely to issue contempt proceedings for the witness to come here, but not in relation to compel a witness to give video testimony. I seem to remember that there was an authority recently in respect of a journalist in Croatia who was subpoenaed, but I would have to look at that to just clarify exactly the circumstances. I did not know Your Honour would be asking that particular question, and I cannot say that it falls on all fours. But there was certainly a Croatian journalist who I believe was subpoenaed. But whether in actual fact that is a contempt for something that he did as opposed to a contempt for refusal, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. Is there anything further, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing, Your Honour, in reply to Mr. Moore. Maybe he wasn't familiar with this, but we did request information from the OTP formally in order to be able to contact this witness, and we received an e-mail that the witness forebade for this information to be disclosed to us. We did request this information and we simply did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just reply to that so that it's absolutely accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It is quite correct that we did receive an e-mail I believe sometime in July or August, but my learned friend prior to that was perfectly capable of looking in a telephone directory --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've made that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would understand that the position of the Defence of Mr. Mrksic is in effect to move that the Chamber should take whatever steps are open to it to compel the attendance of Mr. -- of Witness P019 to give evidence. We have indicated in our earlier observations this morning our appreciation of the general tenor of the evidence so far as it has been disclosed to us, amplified by some remarks of Mr. Domazet. Those indications are essentially of the subject matters about which the witness could speak; they do not indicate or give notice of facts which are directly material to the question of the guilt or innocence of Mr. Mrksic in respect of the particular charges that are brought against him, although they have clear potential relevance to the general circumstances in which it is alleged that those offences occurred. We are not persuaded by what has been put to us, that it is appropriate, therefore, for this Chamber to take any step to compulsorily require the attendance of Witness P019 before the Chamber. Now, that is based upon the -- what is presently known to us about the position and attitude of Witness P019. We will take steps, however, Mr. Domazet to ensure that speedily Witness P019 is formally informed of the potential consequences of his failure to give evidence. We will do that and we'll keep our mind open as to what might be the consequence from his reaction and response to that formal indication. If we were at some time persuaded that we should take action, it would then be important to us to consider the adequacy of the medical certificate and to inquire further into the medical position, hinted at in that certificate. We would indicate clearly that it is our view that that medical certificate does not provide a justification for nonattendance to give evidence. We would at the same time, if we were persuaded to go down that road, look at the alternative option of arranging for the witness to give evidence near his home by videolink to The Hague. If that was a way of affecting and reducing the medical inconvenience if any are demonstrated, we mention those to indicate where we see the questions of the medical certificate and the videolink in our present attitude and position. The normal position, of course, is for the witness to attend, to give evidence, and to be cross-examined, and that is the position whether he's called by the Prosecution or the Defence. We would certainly cooperate and facilitate his nonattendance if he were to give evidence by videolink to obviate any particular risk or any serious other form of inconvenience. But that is not the position that is presently placed before us. I think we have indicated our position sufficiently, and at the moment we will confine ourselves to formal notification to the witness of the potential consequences and we will have regard to any consequences. And we would confirm our earlier indication, Mr. Domazet, that there is no reason why you are not able to speak to the witness whom you wish to call. You have an address for contact, and as Mr. Moore has indicated, there are other means of reaching the witness. You are free to do that. There is no order restraining you in that respect, certainly there was no basis for a restraint once it was made clear by the Prosecution that they were not intending to call that witness. That is our decision in respect of that matter. There is a consequential matter, and that is we had made timetable programming orders in respect that the witness would attend and give evidence and the anticipated time was three days. There therefore is a question of whether it is practical at this stage for the evidence which you proposed to lead, Mr. Borovic, to be advanced from the middle of the week to the beginning of that week, to the Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, do you mean before, an earlier date rather than the one envisaged? Yes, needless to say, we can start right now if you like us to. Whichever date you set, we'll be ready and raring to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We want to save you any difficulty or embarrassment about getting your witnesses here with the needs for passport and visas and some difficulties with the availability of airline seats, all of which we're aware of. So that -- what we will do is advance at the moment the commencement of your case to the Monday of the week that we had previously indicated, so as to minimise any loss of time. And that of course indicates, Mr. Domazet, that we would now anticipate your case to be finished no later than the preceding Friday. Could I also point out, Mr. Domazet, that you may well find that if you do take up our encouragement to speak to the witness, P019, that there may be neither a passport nor a visa. So you need to keep that in mind as well. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, there is one matter I would like to place before the Court, it's to do with the timetable for Mr. Radic's case. As the Court was aware, waivers had been issued as we had been informed on the 7th of September for the witnesses being called on behalf of Mr. Radic. We had applied for those I believe in July. As my learned friends are aware, I was in Belgrade at the end of last week and indeed the start of this week, where I'd hoped to be able to speak to those witnesses in relation to the evidence that they would be giving. Unfortunately, despite what appeared to be the case, that the waivers had been issued on the 7th of September, we were then informed that that had not occurred and that when we -- we therefore could not speak to the witnesses who refused to speak to us because they said they were constrained. We have made inquiries with the department in Belgrade dealing with that issue. We have now been told that the waivers are going to be -- they have to be approved. That will require, apparently, a parliamentary session. That will take two to three weeks, and consequently, not only can I not speak to them, it may create difficulties for the trial to commence. My learned friends know the institutions better than I and indeed I know members of his family are powerful people in that establishment. But the situation, as we now see it with regard to our difficulties, is we've not been able to speak to the witnesses as had been our intention; and that being the case, we still would like to speak to them but cannot do so until the waivers are issued and then you have a problem with regard to translation. As I say, we made an application for a waiver in July. Normally they take two months, for whatever reason - I don't know why, my learned friend may know - they have taken something like four months. So I don't know if my learned friend will be able to assist myself and the Court in relation to that because it clearly will affect the court timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I was going to make an application, and I just forewarn my learned friend that it may well be that I will make an application that if these are witnesses to be called, I would oppose them being called because it may well be suggested by the Prosecution that this is a deliberate ploy to ensure that the Defence -- the Prosecution are unable to speak to these witnesses. But I will not make that application at this time. Hopefully these matters can be clarified by my learned friend's consummate skill and political contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Maybe we have to separate evidence in chief from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, you've heard that issue. I don't ask you to comment on it but if you would discuss the matter with Mr. Moore. It clearly is a looming problem which may even affect the content of evidence you could lead from your witnesses if there has been no waiver by the Government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my learned friend has probably spent a lot of time travelling between The Hague and Belgrade, and he has probably failed to monitor the proceedings here in this courtroom. All my witnesses have already received a waiver of which we have duly informed the OTP. Whether they personally received this document from the relevant services is not something that I'm aware of, but I did tell the people in my office: Were any witnesses to call about any OTP interviews? My answer was always the same. I don't know. I did not wish to interfere. It's up to the witnesses. Under the new rules, I can't affect the course of events. But if it's about the waivers, Mr. Moore could have gotten in touch with the political authorities in my country. He could have collected the documents, and once the witnesses appeared for an interview they could have given the documents to the witnesses. He doesn't have those. Well, that's not my problem, is it? I don't have a single problem with my witnesses formally speaking, nor will they be formally trammeled in any way in their testimony before this Chamber. I am perfectly prepared to assist Mr. Moore in anything outside this, but I should not be expected to take any steps that would be contrary to my client's best interest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, it appears that the information you have received and that which Mr. Borovic has received about waivers by the Serbian government is in conflict. If the two of you would consult each other over the matter, and at the moment we will proceed on the basis, as Mr. Borovic has indicated, that there are in fact waivers in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm very grateful for that, but I regret to say I've had two witnesses come who've specifically said to me that they have not received the waivers and that they were not able to talk. And we did contact the government and told that they had not been handed out. I will speak to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's why I ask you and Mr. Borovic to work together --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- to clarify the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is no other matter. We will now adjourn to resume tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: adjourned at 12.06 p.m.
